source.title: Lasting Effects of Abstract Pretraining Beyond Perplexity
source.authors: Zachary Shinnick; Hemanth Saratchandran; Damien Teney; A. van den Hengel

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether downstream performance tracks pretraining loss by comparing models with abstract pretraining against language-only baselines. It does not test scaling-law fits or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The study reports language-modeling validation-loss comparisons and downstream results, but does not sweep parameter count, tokens, or compute to fit or test power laws. It does not test compute-optimal splits, extrapolation, or architecture-shape effects.
record.test_reason: The study compares models matched on language-pretraining validation loss, differing only in an initial abstract STACK phase or its variants, and shows downstream multi-hop performance differing at comparable or worse loss. This bears on the loss-based half of V6, whether downstream performance follows from pretraining loss. It does not sweep parameters, tokens or compute (only two SmolLM sizes at a fixed 20 tokens/param), so V1–V5, V7 and scale-based V6 are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that early abstract STACK pretraining improves specific capabilities (sequential multi-hop reasoning, deeper DEPO chains) that language-modeling perplexity does not reveal. They add that the gains depend on the abstract data's structure and on initial timing, and persist through billions of language tokens.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses approximately 20 language tokens per parameter as a training budget but does not fit or apply the original scaling-law or compute-optimal allocation method to test it. This is an empirical study of abstract pretraining and downstream transfer.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream outcomes vary with benchmark and model size, abstract-task structure, and when abstract data is introduced. STACK gains are strongest for initial exposure; later or mixed exposure is less effective, and results differ between sequential-chain and merge/comparison task types.
record.code_released: The authors state that code required to reproduce the experiments will be released upon publication; no code URL is stated.
record.problems: Small-scale experiments use SmolLM-135M and 360M; the 360M QA experiments use one pretraining seed due to computational cost. Many plotted results do not have numerical values transcribed in the text. The study does not test scale-based downstream predictability.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant result rows left out.

untested.parts: No sweep of parameters, tokens or compute; no power-law fit.
Uses a 20 tokens/param budget from Hoffmann et al. as a recipe but does not test it.
No shape variation at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fits in other regimes.
Downstream predictability from scale; only two model sizes at a fixed token ratio, with no trend fitted.

missing.what: QUEUE and STACKRAND variants reach validation loss similar to STACK and random init during FineWeb-Edu pretraining, but QA F1 differs: QUEUE is worse than random init, STACKRAND is slightly worse than STACK on MuSiQue. This is loss-matched downstream divergence.
Absolute F1 values for language-only vs STACK at SmolLM-135M (MuSiQue 38.10/41.99, HotpotQA 41.34/43.54, 2WikiMH 50.37/51.24), usable to fill r1–r3.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label was replaced with limits_scope, since matched-loss divergence across interventions qualifies rather than refutes loss-based predictability. The row states were recast so they describe the loss–downstream relation rather than the treatment effect. The results are small-scale, and the 360M results rest on one pretraining seed.

versions.untested_parts: Power-law loss dependence on parameters, tokens, or compute over several orders of magnitude.
Predicting much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocations and their growth with compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests the relationship between pretraining loss and downstream performance for abstract-pretrained versus language-only models; does not test downstream predictability from scale.
Dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting/setup choices, and departures from a single power law.

relationships.condition: Small LMs (SmolLM-135M/360M, 12.7M GPT-2) differing in initialization (STACK, QUEUE, STACKRAND vs random), compared at matched language-token budgets
relationships.reason: Multi-hop QA and DEPO performance differ at comparable or slightly worse LM validation loss, so loss does not predict downstream across initialization interventions (r1–r5, r9–r16 with r7, r8, r17, r18). Text also reports QUEUE at similar loss but worse QA (Sec 5.1). Not a challenge: V6 does not claim loss fixes downstream across different recipes.
relationships.display_finding: Multi-hop question answering and DEPO differed at comparable or slightly worse validation loss, including poorer question answering with QUEUE at similar loss, so loss did not rank initialization interventions.

relationships.reason: Slightly worse loss with unchanged downstream F1 is consistent with loss-based prediction (r6, r8). Single pretraining seed.
relationships.display_finding: Slightly worse loss accompanied unchanged downstream F1 in a single-pretraining-seed comparison.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: STACK-initialized models compared with language-only baselines on tested downstream tasks, alongside their language-modeling validation loss
reader_labels.reason: Downstream QA and DEPO performance improves despite comparable or worse pretraining loss, so the tested loss-based predictability does not hold in these conditions (r1-r5, r7-r18). Scale-based predictability was not tested.
